strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: improving generalization in shared multi-task models. Separately aggregating loss gradients and sharpness corrections is a plausible, modular extension compatible with several existing optimizers.

Experiments cover four gradient aggregation methods and diverse classification and dense-prediction benchmarks. Improvements are broadly consistent: F-CAGrad reduces CelebA error from 8.52 to 8.22 and improves NYUv2 segmentation mIoU from 39.79 to 40.93 while also improving depth and surface-normal metrics.
The supplementary calibration results, perturbation-radius sensitivity, and sharpness measurements provide useful evidence beyond aggregate predictive accuracy.
Algorithm 1 makes the proposed procedure understandable. The manuscript attributes its foundational methods and datasets, and supplies architecture, optimizer, and training-schedule details.
weaknesses: The central contribution is insufficiently isolated experimentally. Missing comparisons include SAM/ASAM applied to a scalarized multi-task loss and direct aggregation of per-task SAM gradients. There are also no component ablations separating the effects of gradient decomposition, shared-parameter perturbations, and task-head perturbations. Consequently, the results do not establish the benefit of the proposed aggregation design beyond established SAM regularization.

Theorem 1 and its formal counterpart, Theorem 4, have unresolved issues. A coordinatewise supremum does not imply that one shared perturbation maximizes every task, as the accompanying interpretation suggests. Appendix A also bounds Gaussian-tail loss contributions using tail probabilities without stating a bounded-loss assumption or another sufficient tail condition. These affect the validity and scope of the theoretical claims.

The connection between the bound and Algorithm 1 is incomplete. The bound jointly perturbs shared and task-specific parameters, whereas the algorithm evaluates these perturbations separately. Furthermore, adding independently aggregated loss and flatness gradients need not decrease both objective families. Equation 5 motivates a surrogate but does not establish the claimed simultaneous improvements for the implemented update.

The experimental method differs from the main description: Appendix B.2 states that adaptive SAM is used, while the algorithm and analysis specify Euclidean SAM. The adaptive update and selected perturbation radii are not documented sufficiently. Tables 2–4 omit variability estimates, and the claimed public implementation has no supplied repository link.

Training cost is not evaluated despite additional task-specific perturbed gradient computations. Runtime, memory, and comparisons under matched computational budgets are particularly relevant to the 40-task CelebA experiment and to assessing practical adoption.

Claims about improving all tasks and addressing negative transfer exceed the evidence. For example, NYUv2 F-MGDA reduces segmentation mIoU from 30.47 to 26.42 despite improving the aggregate score. Although this tradeoff is acknowledged, broader claims should be qualified. The motivating low-resource and noisy-label settings are also not directly tested; parameter-perturbation robustness does not establish robustness in those settings.
